elements.content:
• What is HTML and why it matters

• Build a simple web page – course objectives

• Structure of the lessons

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Maya, and I’m thrilled to start our journey into HTML together. Today we’ll get a quick overview of what this course is all about and why HTML matters.
First, let’s talk about what HTML is and why it’s important. HTML is the language that gives structure to every web page you visit—it’s like the skeleton that holds everything together.
Our main goal for this course is simple: by the end, you’ll be able to build a basic web page from scratch. We’ll walk through each step, from writing tags to seeing your page in a browser.
We’ve organized the lessons into short, hands‑on modules. Each one focuses on a single piece of the puzzle—so you can practice right away and see immediate results.
Let’s keep the pace steady, ask questions whenever something isn’t clear, and celebrate each small win as we go. Ready to dive in?

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Maya, and today we’ll unpack the basic skeleton that every HTML page needs.

First, we start with the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration – it tells the browser this is an HTML document. Next comes the root <html> element that wraps everything. Inside it, the <head> section holds meta‑information like the <title>, which appears on the browser tab. Finally, the <body> section contains all the content you see on the page, such as text, images, and links.
Great job following along! Remember, these four parts – doctype, html, head, and body – are the building blocks for every web page you’ll create.

questions.question: Which of the following tag sequences correctly represents the basic order of elements in an HTML document?
questions.analysis: The correct order is: <!DOCTYPE html> declares the document type, followed by the <html> root element, then the <head> section for metadata, and finally the <body> for page content. All other options place tags in an invalid sequence.

questions.question: Select all tags that are required in a minimal valid HTML5 document (choose all that apply).
questions.analysis: A minimal HTML5 document must include the DOCTYPE declaration, the root <html> element, a <head> section, a <title> element inside <head>, and a <body> element. Omitting any of these makes the document incomplete.

actions.text: Hello everyone! Let’s take a quick quiz to see how well you’ve grasped the basic structure of an HTML document. Read each question carefully, and remember the order we discussed: doctype, html, head, then body.

For the first question, think about the logical flow of a web page. The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration tells the browser what type of document it is, then the <html> element wraps everything, followed by the <head> for meta‑information, and finally the <body> for the page content. That’s the sequence we’re looking for.

The second question asks which tags are absolutely required for a minimal valid HTML5 page. At a minimum you need the doctype, the <html> wrapper, a <head> section, and a <title> inside that head. The <body> tag is optional in the strictest sense, though browsers will add it automatically.

actions.topic: Why is the order of tags and the presence of a title important for browsers and accessibility?
actions.prompt: Think about how a browser parses the document and how screen readers use the title.

elements.content:
• <h1> to <h6> hierarchy

• <p> for paragraphs

• One main heading per page

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's dive into headings and paragraphs in HTML. This is the foundation for structuring any web page.

First, notice the hierarchy of headings from <h1> down to <h6>. Think of them like the titles and subtitles in a book: <h1> is the main title, and the numbers increase as the sections get more specific.

Next, the

tag creates a paragraph. It’s simply a block of text with some space before and after, just like a paragraph in a story.
A best practice to remember: use only one main <h1> per page. It helps browsers and search engines understand the main topic of your page.
Great job! Now you can start building clear, well‑structured pages with headings and paragraphs.

actions.text: Alright, let’s see how well you’ve grasped the basics of headings and paragraphs. Read each question carefully and pick the best answer.
Remember, the main title of a webpage should use the top‑level heading tag, because it signals the most important heading to browsers and search engines.
And when you want to write a regular block of text, you use the paragraph tag, which automatically adds spacing before and after the text.

actions.topic: Why is it important to choose the correct heading level and use paragraph tags appropriately?
actions.prompt: Think about how this affects page structure and readability, then share your thoughts.

elements.content:
• <a href="..."> creates a hyperlink

• <img src="..." alt="..."> embeds an image

• Provide descriptive alt text for accessibility

actions.text: Now let's explore how we add links and images to our web pages.
First, the <a href="..."> tag creates a hyperlink that lets users click to another page or resource.
Notice the href attribute holds the URL—think of it as the address you write on an envelope.
Next, the tag embeds an image. The src points to the image file, and the alt text describes the picture for accessibility.
Always write clear, descriptive alt text—just like you would explain a picture to someone who can't see it.
Great job! With these tags, you can start building richer, more interactive web pages.

questions.analysis: Option A uses the correct <a> tag with the required href attribute and proper closing tag, so it is correct. Options B and C use nonexistent tags or attributes, and D is missing the closing tag and link text.

actions.text: Alright, let’s check what we just covered about links and images. This quick quiz will help you see if you can spot the right HTML syntax and remember the key attributes.

For the first question, think about the basic structure of an anchor tag: the tag name is **a**, the link URL goes in the **href** attribute, and the text you want visitors to click appears between the opening and closing tags. Any extra attributes are fine, but the **href** is the must‑have for a functional link.

The second question asks for the required attribute(s) of an **img** element. Remember, an image needs a **src** attribute so the browser knows where to fetch the picture, and an **alt** attribute to provide alternative text for accessibility and cases when the image can’t load.

actions.topic: Why are the **href**, **src**, and **alt** attributes so important in HTML?
actions.prompt: Share a real‑world example of when missing one of these attributes could cause a problem.

elements.content: Explain how to create bullet and numbered lists.
• Nested lists using additional <ul> or <ol>

actions.text: Hello everyone, I’m Maya. Today we’ll learn how to make both unordered and ordered lists in HTML, so you can organize information clearly on your web pages.
First, an unordered list uses the <ul> tag with <li> items inside. Each <li> becomes a bullet point, perfect for items that don’t need a specific sequence.
Next, an ordered list uses the <ol> tag together with <li>. The browser automatically numbers each <li>, which is great for steps or ranked items.
Finally, you can nest lists by placing another <ul> or <ol> inside an <li>. This lets you create sub‑lists, like a list of tasks with sub‑tasks underneath.

questions.analysis: The <ul> tag defines an unordered (bulleted) list. <ol> is for ordered lists, <li> is used for each list item, and <div> is a generic container.

actions.text: Hello everyone! I'm Ms. Maya Hart. Let’s take a quick quiz to see how well we’ve mastered HTML lists. Read each question carefully and pick the best answer.

Remember, the <ul> tag is the container for an unordered (bulleted) list, while <ol> is for an ordered (numbered) list. Inside either container, each individual item must be wrapped in an <li> tag—that’s the only tag that belongs directly inside the list.

A common slip is to place paragraph or div tags straight inside <ul> or <ol>. Those tags belong inside the <li> elements, not as direct children of the list container. Keep that structure in mind as you choose your answers.

actions.topic: Why is it important to use <li> tags inside lists, and what problems might arise if we skip them?
actions.prompt: Think about how browsers render lists and how screen readers interpret them.

elements.content:
• <table> → container for rows

• <tr> → table row

• <th> (header) vs <td> (data) cells

• Simple example: <table><tr><th>Name</th><td>Alice</td></tr></table>

actions.text: Now let's explore HTML tables. A table lets us display data in rows and columns, just like a spreadsheet.
First, we use the <table> tag as the container. Inside it, each <tr> defines a row. Within a row, <th> creates a header cell and <td> creates a regular data cell.
Notice the difference between <th> and <td>—headers describe the column, while data cells hold the actual values.
Here's a simple example: a table with a header row for "Name" and "Age", followed by two data rows. When you write this markup, the browser will line everything up nicely.
To recap, remember the hierarchy: <table> contains <tr>, which in turn contains <th> for headers and <td> for data. That's the foundation for building any table in HTML.

questions.question: Which HTML tag is missing to properly close a table row?
questions.analysis: The closing tag for a table row is . starts a row, while ends it. defines a cell and ends the whole table.

questions.question: Match each HTML table tag with its purpose (select all that apply).
questions.analysis: Correct: <table> starts the table, <th> marks a header cell, and <td> marks a normal data cell. <tr> defines a table row, not a column; therefore option C is incorrect.

actions.text: Alright, let’s see how well you’ve grasped the basics of HTML tables. Read each question carefully and pick the answer that fits.
For the first question, think about the structure of a table row. After you open a row with <tr>, what tag do you need to close it?
The second question asks you to match each tag with its purpose. Remember: <table> holds the whole table, <tr> creates a new row, <th> is for header cells, and <td> is for regular data cells.
Take a moment, review the options, and choose the answers that best describe each tag’s role.

actions.topic: Why is it important to use the correct closing tags and match tags to their functions when building a table?
actions.prompt: Think about how browsers render the table and how it affects what users see.

elements.content:
• <form> container

• Input types: text, email, submit

• <label> association

• <textarea> and <button> elements

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into HTML Forms – the way we gather information from users on a web page.
First, the <form> tag acts like a container that holds all the input fields you want to collect.
Inside a form you can use different input types—text for names, email for addresses, and a submit button to send the data.
Remember to pair each input with a <label> element; this tells screen readers what the field is for and makes clicking the label focus the input.
You can also add a <textarea> for longer messages and a <button> element for custom actions beyond the default submit.
Great job! That covers the basic building blocks of HTML forms. Try creating a simple contact form on your own and see how each piece fits together.

questions.question: Which HTML input type should be used to let the user enter a password that is masked on the screen?
questions.analysis: The 'password' input type masks characters as they are typed, protecting the password from onlookers. The other types display text plainly.

questions.question: In a well‑structured form, which element correctly associates the text label "Email" with its input field?
questions.analysis: The <label> element with a 'for' attribute matching the input's id creates an explicit association, improving accessibility. Option C follows this pattern; the others do not provide a proper link.

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! Let's put our new form skills to the test with a quick quiz. Read each question carefully and choose the best answer.
Remember, the right input type helps the browser know what kind of data to expect, and linking a label to its input makes the form accessible for everyone.
Take a moment, then submit your answers. Don't worry if you're not sure—just give it your best shot!

actions.topic: Why is it important to match a label with its input field, and how does the correct input type improve user experience?
actions.prompt: Share any thoughts or questions you have about labeling and input types.

elements.content:
• Sectioning elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Improves SEO and aids screen readers

• Replace generic <div> with meaningful tags

actions.text: Alright, let’s dive into Semantic HTML. This helps us give our web pages a clear, meaningful structure.
First, we have sectioning elements like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. Think of them as the different rooms in a house, each with a specific purpose.
Using these tags tells search engines and screen‑readers exactly what each part of the page does, which improves SEO and accessibility.
Finally, replace generic <div> containers with these meaningful tags whenever possible. It’s like labeling boxes so you know what’s inside without opening them.
Great job! Now you can see how a few simple tags make your HTML both friendlier to users and easier for machines to understand.

elements.content:
• Use meaningful headings

• Add descriptive alt text to images

• Indent code for readability

• Keep structure logical and consistent

actions.text: Let's look at the slide titled Good Practices, which outlines habits for clean, maintainable HTML.

First, use meaningful headings so both people and search engines understand the page structure. Next, add descriptive alt text to every image; this helps users who rely on screen readers. Then, indent your code consistently—proper indentation makes it much easier to follow the nesting of tags. Finally, keep the overall structure logical and consistent, grouping related sections together and using the same naming conventions throughout.
These simple steps might seem small, but they make a big difference in readability and future maintenance.
To recap, remember headings, alt text, indentation, and a logical layout as your checklist for tidy HTML.

questions.question: Which HTML tag defines the overall structure of a web page?
questions.analysis: The <html> tag encloses the entire document. <head> contains metadata, <body> contains page content, and <div> is a generic container.

questions.question: Which element is used to create a hyperlink to another page?
questions.analysis: The <a> element with an href attribute creates a clickable link. <link> is for external resources, <nav> defines navigation sections, and <href> is not a standalone tag.

questions.question: Select all tags that are considered semantic HTML5 elements (choose two).
questions.analysis: <section> and <article> provide meaning about the content they contain. <div> and <span> are non‑semantic containers.

questions.question: Which attribute is required to display an image stored in the file "photo.jpg"?
questions.analysis: The src attribute of the tag specifies the image file location. href is for links, alt provides alternative text, and path is not a valid attribute.

questions.question: Which of the following are valid ways to create an ordered list? (select all that apply)
questions.analysis: <ol> defines an ordered (numbered) list. <ul> creates an unordered list, and the custom <list> tag is not standard HTML.

questions.question: Which tag should be used to group related form controls together for better accessibility?
questions.analysis: <fieldset> groups related controls and can contain a <legend>. The other tags do not provide this semantic grouping for forms.

questions.question: Explain why using semantic tags (like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>) is important for web accessibility and SEO.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Describes how semantic tags convey meaning to assistive technologies – 40% (2) Shows impact on search‑engine indexing and ranking – 30% (3) Uses clear language and gives at least one concrete example – 30%
questions.analysis: Good answers mention that semantic tags give structure that screen readers can navigate, help crawlers understand page hierarchy, and improve SEO. Examples such as using <nav> for navigation links or <main> for primary content are expected.

questions.question: List three best practices when creating HTML tables for data presentation, and briefly describe each.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Mentions use of <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> for structure – 35% (2) Includes descriptive <caption> and proper <th> for headers – 35% (3) Addresses accessibility (e.g., scope attribute, ARIA) – 30%
questions.analysis: A complete answer includes: (a) using table sections to separate header, body, and footer; (b) providing a clear caption and using <th> for column/row headings; (c) adding scope attributes or ARIA labels so assistive tech can interpret relationships.

actions.text: Alright everyone, it's time for our final review quiz! We'll go through a handful of questions that cover the whole page we just studied—document structure, links, images, lists, tables, forms, and semantic tags. Read each question carefully, pick the best answer, and remember the key ideas we discussed.

When you see a question about the overall page layout, think of the tag that wraps everything – that's the <html> element. For hyperlinks, recall that the clickable part is the <a> tag, not <link> or <href>. And whenever an image is shown, the src attribute points to the file, while alt provides a description for accessibility.

Semantic HTML5 tags like <section> and <article> give meaning to the content, helping screen readers and search engines understand the page structure. Tags such as <div> and <span> are generic containers, so they aren't considered semantic. Grouping form controls with <fieldset> improves accessibility by creating a clear boundary and optional legend.

For lists, an ordered list always uses the <ol> element with <li> items inside. Unordered lists use <ul>. Anything else, like a custom <list> tag, won't be recognized by browsers. And when building tables, remember to use <thead>, <tbody>, and <th> for headers, keep the layout simple, and add captions or summaries for context.

actions.topic: How do semantic tags improve both accessibility and SEO, and which best practices for tables will you apply in your next project?
actions.prompt: Share one example of a semantic tag you plan to use and one table tip you found most helpful.

Remember, the <ul> tag is the container for an unordered (bulleted) list, while <ol> is for an ordered (numbered) list. Inside either container, each individual item must be wrapped in an <li> tag—that’s the only tag that belongs directly inside the list.

A common slip is to place paragraph or div tags straight inside <ul> or <ol>. Those tags belong inside the <li> elements, not as direct children of the list container. Keep that structure in mind as you choose your answers.

blocks.label: Slide content block 2
blocks.html:
• <table> → container for rows

• <tr> → table row

• <th> (header) vs <td> (data) cells

• Simple example: <table><tr><th>Name</th><td>Alice</td></tr></table>
blocks.plainText: • <table> → container for rows • <tr> → table row • <th> (header) vs <td> (data) cells • Simple example: <table><tr><th>Name</th><td>Alice</td></tr></table>

blocks.text: Now let's explore HTML tables. A table lets us display data in rows and columns, just like a spreadsheet.
First, we use the <table> tag as the container. Inside it, each <tr> defines a row. Within a row, <th> creates a header cell and <td> creates a regular data cell.
Notice the difference between <th> and <td>—headers describe the column, while data cells hold the actual values.
Here's a simple example: a table with a header row for "Name" and "Age", followed by two data rows. When you write this markup, the browser will line everything up nicely.
To recap, remember the hierarchy: <table> contains <tr>, which in turn contains <th> for headers and <td> for data. That's the foundation for building any table in HTML.

blocks.question: Which HTML tag is missing to properly close a table row?
blocks.explanation: The closing tag for a table row is . starts a row, while ends it. defines a cell and ends the whole table.

blocks.question: Match each HTML table tag with its purpose (select all that apply).
blocks.explanation: Correct: <table> starts the table, <th> marks a header cell, and <td> marks a normal data cell. <tr> defines a table row, not a column; therefore option C is incorrect.

blocks.text: Alright, let’s see how well you’ve grasped the basics of HTML tables. Read each question carefully and pick the answer that fits.
For the first question, think about the structure of a table row. After you open a row with <tr>, what tag do you need to close it?
The second question asks you to match each tag with its purpose. Remember: <table> holds the whole table, <tr> creates a new row, <th> is for header cells, and <td> is for regular data cells.
Take a moment, review the options, and choose the answers that best describe each tag’s role.

blocks.label: Slide content block 2
blocks.html:
• <form> container

• Input types: text, email, submit

• <label> association

• <textarea> and <button> elements
blocks.plainText: • <form> container • Input types: text , email , submit • <label> association • <textarea> and <button> elements

blocks.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into HTML Forms – the way we gather information from users on a web page.
First, the <form> tag acts like a container that holds all the input fields you want to collect.
Inside a form you can use different input types—text for names, email for addresses, and a submit button to send the data.
Remember to pair each input with a <label> element; this tells screen readers what the field is for and makes clicking the label focus the input.
You can also add a <textarea> for longer messages and a <button> element for custom actions beyond the default submit.
Great job! That covers the basic building blocks of HTML forms. Try creating a simple contact form on your own and see how each piece fits together.

blocks.question: Which HTML input type should be used to let the user enter a password that is masked on the screen?
blocks.explanation: The 'password' input type masks characters as they are typed, protecting the password from onlookers. The other types display text plainly.

blocks.question: In a well‑structured form, which element correctly associates the text label "Email" with its input field?
blocks.explanation: The <label> element with a 'for' attribute matching the input's id creates an explicit association, improving accessibility. Option C follows this pattern; the others do not provide a proper link.

blocks.text: Good morning, everyone! Let's put our new form skills to the test with a quick quiz. Read each question carefully and choose the best answer.
Remember, the right input type helps the browser know what kind of data to expect, and linking a label to its input makes the form accessible for everyone.
Take a moment, then submit your answers. Don't worry if you're not sure—just give it your best shot!

blocks.label: Slide content block 2
blocks.html:
• Sectioning elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Improves SEO and aids screen readers

• Replace generic <div> with meaningful tags
blocks.plainText: • Sectioning elements: <header> , <nav> , <main> , <section> , <article> , <footer> • Improves SEO and aids screen readers • Replace generic <div> with meaningful tags

blocks.text: Alright, let’s dive into Semantic HTML. This helps us give our web pages a clear, meaningful structure.
First, we have sectioning elements like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. Think of them as the different rooms in a house, each with a specific purpose.
Using these tags tells search engines and screen‑readers exactly what each part of the page does, which improves SEO and accessibility.
Finally, replace generic <div> containers with these meaningful tags whenever possible. It’s like labeling boxes so you know what’s inside without opening them.
Great job! Now you can see how a few simple tags make your HTML both friendlier to users and easier for machines to understand.

blocks.label: Slide content block 2
blocks.html:
• Use meaningful headings

• Add descriptive alt text to images

• Indent code for readability

• Keep structure logical and consistent
blocks.plainText: • Use meaningful headings • Add descriptive alt text to images • Indent code for readability • Keep structure logical and consistent

blocks.text: Let's look at the slide titled Good Practices, which outlines habits for clean, maintainable HTML.

First, use meaningful headings so both people and search engines understand the page structure. Next, add descriptive alt text to every image; this helps users who rely on screen readers. Then, indent your code consistently—proper indentation makes it much easier to follow the nesting of tags. Finally, keep the overall structure logical and consistent, grouping related sections together and using the same naming conventions throughout.
These simple steps might seem small, but they make a big difference in readability and future maintenance.
To recap, remember headings, alt text, indentation, and a logical layout as your checklist for tidy HTML.

blocks.question: Which HTML tag defines the overall structure of a web page?
blocks.explanation: The <html> tag encloses the entire document. <head> contains metadata, <body> contains page content, and <div> is a generic container.

blocks.question: Which element is used to create a hyperlink to another page?
blocks.explanation: The <a> element with an href attribute creates a clickable link. <link> is for external resources, <nav> defines navigation sections, and <href> is not a standalone tag.

blocks.question: Select all tags that are considered semantic HTML5 elements (choose two).
blocks.explanation: <section> and <article> provide meaning about the content they contain. <div> and <span> are non‑semantic containers.

blocks.question: Which attribute is required to display an image stored in the file "photo.jpg"?
blocks.explanation: The src attribute of the tag specifies the image file location. href is for links, alt provides alternative text, and path is not a valid attribute.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid ways to create an ordered list? (select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: <ol> defines an ordered (numbered) list. <ul> creates an unordered list, and the custom <list> tag is not standard HTML.

blocks.question: Which tag should be used to group related form controls together for better accessibility?
blocks.explanation: <fieldset> groups related controls and can contain a <legend>. The other tags do not provide this semantic grouping for forms.

blocks.question: Explain why using semantic tags (like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>) is important for web accessibility and SEO.
blocks.explanation: Good answers mention that semantic tags give structure that screen readers can navigate, help crawlers understand page hierarchy, and improve SEO. Examples such as using <nav> for navigation links or <main> for primary content are expected.

blocks.question: List three best practices when creating HTML tables for data presentation, and briefly describe each.
blocks.explanation: A complete answer includes: (a) using table sections to separate header, body, and footer; (b) providing a clear caption and using <th> for column/row headings; (c) adding scope attributes or ARIA labels so assistive tech can interpret relationships.

blocks.text: Alright everyone, it's time for our final review quiz! We'll go through a handful of questions that cover the whole page we just studied—document structure, links, images, lists, tables, forms, and semantic tags. Read each question carefully, pick the best answer, and remember the key ideas we discussed.

When you see a question about the overall page layout, think of the tag that wraps everything – that's the <html> element. For hyperlinks, recall that the clickable part is the <a> tag, not <link> or <href>. And whenever an image is shown, the src attribute points to the file, while alt provides a description for accessibility.

Semantic HTML5 tags like <section> and <article> give meaning to the content, helping screen readers and search engines understand the page structure. Tags such as <div> and <span> are generic containers, so they aren't considered semantic. Grouping form controls with <fieldset> improves accessibility by creating a clear boundary and optional legend.

For lists, an ordered list always uses the <ol> element with <li> items inside. Unordered lists use <ul>. Anything else, like a custom <list> tag, won't be recognized by browsers. And when building tables, remember to use <thead>, <tbody>, and <th> for headers, keep the layout simple, and add captions or summaries for context.
